title: Number of Changing Keys
statement:
Someone typed the string `s` on a keyboard, one character after another. Each letter lives on one key whatever its case, because Shift and Caps Lock are not keys that count here: `'q'` and `'Q'` come from the same key.

A key change happens whenever a character is typed on a different key from the character just before it. Return how many key changes happen while `s` is typed.
constraints: s contains only English letters, lowercase and uppercase.
notes:
## Intuition

Only neighbouring characters matter: each adjacent pair either stays on the same key or changes it. Two characters share a key exactly when they are the same letter ignoring case, so convert the whole string to lowercase once and then compare plain characters.

## Approach

1. Lowercase `s` into `keys`, so every character names its key.
2. Start `changes` at 0.
3. For every index `i` from 1 onward, compare `keys[i]` with `keys[i - 1]`; if they differ, a new key was pressed, so add 1.
4. Return `changes`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aAbBcC"` becomes `keys = "aabbcc"`. The pairs are `a,a` (same), `a,b` (change, 1), `b,b` (same), `b,c` (change, 2) and `c,c` (same). The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the string after lowercasing it.
- Space: O(n) for the lowercased copy (O(1) if you compare case-insensitively in place).

## Pitfalls

- `'a'` followed by `'A'` is not a change; comparing the raw characters counts it wrongly.
- Count changes between neighbours, not distinct letters: `"aba"` has 2 changes even though it uses 2 keys.
- A one-character string has no pairs, so the answer is 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `keys` | `s` in lowercase: the key behind each character |
| `changes` | key changes counted so far |
| `i` | index of the character compared with the one before it |

narration.3: Lowercase the string so that each character simply names the key it was typed on.
narration.4: No key changes have been seen yet.
narration.5: Look at every character after the first, together with the one before it.
narration.7: Yes: that is one more key change.
narration.10: Every adjacent pair has been checked; return the count.
